blocks.prompt: The Ant That Left a Message
blocks.text: One ant found a crumb of bread. It was too big to carry alone. So the ant walked home. As it walked, it dabbed a smell onto the ground. Drop by drop, it made a smell trail. Back at the nest, the other ants tapped it with their antennae. They smelled the trail. Then they followed it, one behind the other, all the way to the bread. Ants cannot shout. They do not need to. They leave messages made of smell, and the whole nest can read them.

a smell trail

blocks.prompt: The Town Under Your Feet
blocks.text: Under the ground, a nest of ants is busy. Dig it up and you would find rooms and tunnels, hundreds of them, joined together like a tiny underground town. One ant in the nest is much bigger than the rest. She is the queen. Her job is to lay eggs, and she does almost nothing else. Nearly every other ant in the nest is one of her daughters. The workers do everything. Some clean the tunnels. Some feed the babies. Some carry out the trash. Some go outside to hunt for food. When a worker finds food, she leaves a smell trail so the others can follow her back to it. Ants have no ears and most have weak eyes. They talk with smell instead. Those two feelers on an ant's head are called antennae, and they are packed with smell sensors. When two ants meet, they touch antennae. In one quick tap, they learn who the other ant is, which nest she is from, and whether she has found food.

blocks.prompt: The Ants That Grow Their Own Food
blocks.text: In the forests of Central and South America, a line of leaves marches across the ground. Look closer. Under each leaf is an ant. These are leafcutter ants, and they are farmers. A worker climbs a tree, cuts a piece of leaf with her jaws, and carries it home. The piece can weigh several times more than she does. A big colony can strip a whole tree in a night. Here is the strange part. The ants do not eat the leaves. They cannot digest them. Instead they chew the leaves into a soft pulp and spread the pulp in dark underground gardens. On that pulp they grow a fungus, something like a mushroom. The fungus is the food. The ants feed it, weed it, and eat it, and it grows nowhere else on Earth without them. Farming brings farming problems. A mold called Escovopsis attacks the gardens and can kill them. So the ants carry a defense on their own bodies: a pale bacteria that grows in patches on their skin and makes a natural antibiotic. When a garden gets infected, the ants dose it. A leafcutter colony can hold several million ants, and the workers come in sizes. The largest have jaws that can slice through leather. The smallest ride along on the leaf pieces, guarding the carrier from flies that would lay eggs on her. Humans started farming about twelve thousand years ago. Ants have been growing fungus gardens for roughly fifty million.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About 20 quadrillion ants are alive right now

Army ants build bridges from their own bodies
No ant is in charge, not even the queen
Ant behavior inspired real computer algorithms

blocks.prompt: Nobody Is In Charge
blocks.text: There is no ant in charge. That is the first thing to understand, and it is harder to accept than it sounds. A colony has a queen, but a queen is not a boss. She does not give orders, plan the day, or know what is happening twenty feet away in a tunnel. She lays eggs. Nothing more. Every clever thing a colony does, the trails, the gardens, the wars, the bridges, is done by workers who each follow a handful of simple rules and understand nothing of the whole. Watch army ants and the trick becomes visible. Army ants of the species Eciton burchellii do not dig a permanent nest. They march, hundreds of thousands of them, and at night they build a shelter called a bivouac out of nothing but their own bodies, hooking leg to leg into living walls around the queen and the young. Come morning it dissolves and the column moves on. On the march they meet gaps. A gap in a trail slows everyone down, so an ant that finds one stops and holds still. Another crawls over her and stops too. Ant by ant, a bridge of bodies grows across the gap, and the column pours over it. The bridge even adjusts itself. If the crossing gets busy, more ants join and it widens. If traffic thins, the ants at the edges feel fewer footsteps, let go, and rejoin the march. No ant measured the gap. No ant decided to build. Each one followed a rule roughly like this: if ants are walking on me, freeze; if they stop walking on me, leave. Simple rules, repeated by millions, add up to something that looks like intelligence. Scientists call it swarm intelligence, and they now copy it in software that routes delivery trucks and internet traffic. It is worth knowing how much of this is happening under your feet. A study published in 2022 estimated that about twenty thousand trillion ants are alive on Earth right now. Weigh all of them together and they outweigh every wild bird and every wild mammal on the planet combined.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Cataglyphis fortis, the Saharan desert ant
Forages at midday when the ground is lethal
Navigates by polarized skylight and step counting
An ant brain holds about 250,000 neurons
Tested in 2006 with stilts made of pig bristle
Robot designers borrow its dead reckoning

blocks.prompt: The Ant That Counts Its Own Steps
blocks.text: In the salt pans of Tunisia there is very little to look at. The ground is flat, pale, and cracked, and in summer it reaches temperatures that would cook most animals in minutes. Which is exactly why Cataglyphis fortis, the Saharan desert ant, goes out at midday. Her food is other insects that have already died of the heat, and the lizards and spiders that would eat her are hiding. She has a problem. Her nest is a hole in the ground about the width of a pencil, with no mound, no marker, and nothing nearby to recognize. She cannot lay a smell trail, because on ground that hot the scent boils away almost as fast as she can leave it. And she does not walk in a straight line. A foraging ant loops and zigzags across the pan for a hundred meters or more, hunting. Then she finds a dead fly, picks it up, turns, and runs almost dead straight back to a pencil-width hole she cannot see, and she hits it. The name for this is path integration. As she wanders, the ant is quietly keeping a running total: which way am I facing, and how far have I come. Direction is the easier half. She reads the pattern of polarized light in the sky, which a special patch of her eye can see and we cannot, and uses it as a compass even when the sun itself is behind a cloud. The hard half is distance. Nothing in the desert tells her how far she has walked. So she counts her own steps. That claim sounds absurd, and for a long time it was only a hypothesis. In 2006, three researchers named Matthias Wittlinger, Rudiger Wehner and Harald Wolf tested it in the least subtle way imaginable. They let ants walk from the nest to a feeder. Then, at the feeder, they changed the ants' legs. Some got stilts, tiny lengths of pig bristle glued to their feet. Others had the ends of their legs trimmed, leaving stumps. The results were exactly what a step counter predicts. The ants on stilts, taking longer strides than their brains expected, ran straight past the nest and began searching in empty ground beyond it. The ants on stumps, taking shorter strides, stopped short and searched in front of it. Neither group was confused about direction. Both were wrong about distance, and wrong by roughly the amount their stride length had changed. Then came the part that settled it. The researchers let the altered ants make a full round trip on their new legs. This time they went home accurately. Given one outbound journey to measure the world with the legs they now had, they recalibrated. The counter was not broken. It had simply been fed the wrong stride. An ant brain holds around a quarter of a million neurons. A human brain holds roughly eighty-six billion. With that quarter of a million, on a burning salt pan, a desert ant runs a compass, an odometer, and the arithmetic that turns a hundred meters of zigzag into one straight line home. Engineers who build robots for places where satellite navigation fails, caves, mines, the ocean floor, keep coming back to this ant. She is doing, on a budget of almost nothing, the exact thing they cannot yet do well.
